title: Northbridge Health x Redwood — post-enable check-in (throttling protections)
summary: Customer success check-in after enabling hot-route capacity protection for Northbridge Health. Customer observed intermittent 429s on a single high-traffic chat route during a burst/retry storm and wants clarity on semantics, Retry-After usage, and recommended retry/concurrency behavior. Redwood reviewed reason codes, the difference between per-tenant/per-route limits vs overload shedding, and how enterprise priority lanes behave during regional capacity dips. Agreed on tuning burst settings for one route, plus customer-side changes to reduce synchronized retries.
topics: Observed 429 patterns after protections enabled (time of day, regions, endpoints)
429 semantics: quota vs rate limit vs overload
Retry-After header behavior and client retry strategy (backoff + jitter)
Concurrency controls (max in-flight, streaming vs non-streaming)
Enterprise lane expectations during regional degradation and failover
Next steps: limit tuning + follow-up after client change
action_items: Redwood (Rafael): Pull lane health + throttling metrics for /v1/chat/completions route for Northbridge Health for 2025-02-04 19:00–21:00 UTC; share a short readout with reason code breakdown.
Redwood (Nikhil): Send customer-facing explanation of 429 reason codes + recommended retry guidance (include Retry-After and max retry attempts).
Customer (Erin): Adjust client to honor Retry-After, add exponential backoff with jitter, and cap concurrent retries per user/session; report results by next check-in.
Redwood (Liam): Coordinate a temporary burst increase for the single hot route in us-east-1 while customer rolls out retry fixes; confirm updated policy window.
Customer (Miguel): Provide current gateway timeout/retry settings (Envoy/SDK) and whether they do hedged requests; send config snippet in email.
next_steps: Redwood to share metrics + proposed limit tweak within 1 business day
Customer to deploy retry/backoff changes to staging by early next week
Schedule 30-min follow-up to confirm 429 rate reduction and adjust limits if needed
transcript:
Meeting: Northbridge Health x Redwood — post-enable check-in (throttling protections)
Recorded: 2025-02-06 17:00 UTC
Duration: 38 min
Attendees (Redwood): Liam O'Rourke, Rafael Mendes, Nikhil Sharma
Attendees (Northbridge Health): Erin Wallace, Miguel Santos, Priya Desai

Auto-Summary (Fireflies):
- Reviewed new throttling protections enabled for Northbridge Health’s hot chat route.
- Discussed intermittent 429 spikes and how Retry-After should be used.
- Agreed on short-term burst tuning + customer-side retry/concurrency adjustments.


[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Cool, alright. Hey everyone. Thanks for making time. This is our post-enable check-in on the capacity protection stuff we turned on last week for your account. Goal today is: what you’re seeing, what’s confusing, and if we need to tune anything.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Sounds good.

[00:20] Erin Wallace: Yep.

[00:22] Miguel Santos: Yep, thanks.

[00:25] Liam O'Rourke: Quick intros on our side—I'm Liam, your TAM. Rafael from SRE is here, he’s been on the rollout side, and Nikhil is PM for the hosted API semantics.

[00:36] Nikhil Sharma: Hey.

[00:38] Rafael Mendes: Hi everyone.

[00:41] Liam O'Rourke: Erin, do you want to start with what you noticed after we enabled it?

[00:46] Erin Wallace: Sure. So overall things feel stable, like we didn’t see the big tail latency spikes we had during that incident in January. But we did see 429s, and it was a bit surprising because, like, we thought the “enterprise lane” meant we basically wouldn’t see 429 unless we were truly, like, over our contract. That’s probably our misunderstanding.

[01:09] Erin Wallace: The pattern: mostly on our primary endpoint, which is /v1/chat/completions. It’s the one the clinician app uses. We saw a burst around, um, Tuesday evening UTC. Our logs show about 1.5% 429 for about 12 minutes, then it went away.

[01:28] Miguel Santos: And we saw it in us-east-1 mostly. eu-west-1 was lower, but not zero.

[01:36] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. Do you have the approximate time window?

[01:39] Erin Wallace: 19:20 to 19:32 UTC, Feb 4th.

[01:44] Rafael Mendes: Okay, that helps.

[01:46] Liam O'Rourke: And did the 429 responses include a Retry-After header on your side?

[01:52] Erin Wallace: Sometimes. Not consistently. That’s one of the things we wanted to ask about.

[01:58] Nikhil Sharma: That’s very useful feedback. It should be consistent, but there are a couple code paths depending on where the throttle happens. We’ve been standardizing those.

[02:09] Miguel Santos: Yeah and also the body has, like, a reason string. I saw “rate_limit” and I saw “over_capacity” at least once. Again, not sure if that’s two different things.

[02:23] Rafael Mendes: It is, yeah. Let me try to break down the taxonomy, and then we can map it to what you saw.

[02:29] Rafael Mendes: There are basically three buckets that can yield 429 in our system right now:
1) Per-tenant/per-route rate limit (think requests-per-second with optional burst)
2) Quota enforcement (daily/monthly units) — that’s rarer and usually comes with a different message
3) Overload shedding—when the fleet or a region is saturated and we’re preserving capacity for higher-priority traffic.

[02:55] Rafael Mendes: The “enterprise lane” concept helps most with #3. It doesn’t eliminate #1 because #1 is there to protect you from your own retry storms and to give you predictable behavior.

[03:07] Erin Wallace: Okay, so it’s not like “no throttling,” it’s “throttling is more predictable and we don’t get drowned out by self-serve.”

[03:14] Rafael Mendes: Exactly.

[03:17] Priya Desai: That’s helpful framing.

[03:20] Liam O'Rourke: Erin, when you saw the burst, was that tied to a deploy on your end or some downstream issue that would cause retries?

[03:28] Erin Wallace: We did have an internal network issue earlier that day. And our client has a retry policy that is maybe… aggressive. It retries 5 times, and I think it retries quickly.

[03:41] Miguel Santos: The default in our gateway is like immediate retry on 429 for the first one. Which, in hindsight, is… not ideal.

[03:49] Nikhil Sharma: Yeah, on 429 specifically, immediate retry tends to turn a small throttle into a synchronized storm.

[03:56] Erin Wallace: Yeah.

[03:58] Liam O'Rourke: This is the “retry shape” problem we’ve been trying to address with the new semantics. Can I ask—are you using streaming responses on that route?

[04:06] Erin Wallace: We’re mixed. The clinician app uses streaming. Some back-office batch uses non-streaming.

[04:12] Nikhil Sharma: Streaming is generally better for perceived latency, but it does keep a connection open longer, which can make concurrency limits matter more. Not saying it’s the cause here, but it’s part of the picture.

[04:24] Miguel Santos: The 429s were more on non-streaming, I think. But I need to confirm.

[04:29] Rafael Mendes: If you can confirm that, it’s helpful. In our system, non-streaming calls can show up as higher instantaneous “request pressure” because they’re shorter but more frequent.

[04:41] Liam O'Rourke: On the Retry-After thing—Nikhil, can you clarify what the client should do?

[04:46] Nikhil Sharma: Sure. If you get a 429 and there is Retry-After, treat it as authoritative. Wait that long before retrying. If Retry-After is absent, use exponential backoff with jitter. The big thing is: don’t have all clients wait 200ms and then retry at the same time.

[05:05] Nikhil Sharma: Also cap total attempts. We generally recommend 2-3 retries max for interactive traffic, and maybe more for offline batch, but with a longer ceiling and circuit breaker behavior.

[05:16] Erin Wallace: Right now we do 5 and the first two are basically immediate.

[05:20] Miguel Santos: And no jitter.

[05:22] Erin Wallace: So, we can fix that.

[05:25] Liam O'Rourke: Great.

[05:26] Priya Desai: Can you also clarify “over_capacity” vs “rate_limit”? Like, does it matter for how we retry?

[05:34] Rafael Mendes: It does. “rate_limit” means you exceeded the configured RPS or concurrency policy for that route. Retrying immediately won’t help unless your traffic is bursting and then calm. “over_capacity” means the region or lane is saturated; in that case, Retry-After usually is longer and it’s more likely you should do failover or degrade if you can.

[05:57] Miguel Santos: We do have region failover, but it’s based on 5xx rates. We don’t currently trigger it on 429.

[06:03] Rafael Mendes: That’s a good point. I wouldn’t recommend failing over on every 429 because rate_limit is per-region, but it’s not always “go elsewhere.” However, if you get “over_capacity” and it persists, region failover can help, assuming your data residency rules allow it.

[06:20] Erin Wallace: We can fail over between us-east and eu-west for this workload, yes.

[06:25] Nikhil Sharma: Another option is degrade within a region: e.g., reduce max_tokens, or switch to a smaller model, if you have that logic.

[06:34] Erin Wallace: We can reduce max_tokens. We don’t have model switching yet. We’ve discussed it.

[06:41] Liam O'Rourke: That ties to a “graceful degradation” pattern. We can share guidance there too.

[06:46] Miguel Santos: Coming back to “Retry-After inconsistent”—is that expected, or is it a bug?

[06:52] Nikhil Sharma: It’s partially a bug, partially rollout state. The gateway path always sets it. The router path historically didn’t for some reason codes. We’ve been standardizing. For enterprise protections, we’re aiming to have it everywhere.

[07:09] Rafael Mendes: For the window you gave, it might be a mix: some 429 at the gateway due to per-route limit and some at the router due to overload signals.

[07:19] Erin Wallace: That would explain seeing two different bodies.

[07:23] Liam O'Rourke: Miguel, do you know if your client logs include the request ID headers? That would let Rafael correlate.

[07:28] Miguel Santos: Yes, we log x-request-id and the region.

[07:33] Rafael Mendes: Perfect. If you can send like 20 sample request IDs from that burst, I can map it quickly.

[07:40] Miguel Santos: Yep, can do.

[07:42] Priya Desai: So, question: when you say “per-route limit,” is that something we can see and change, or is it fixed?

[07:49] Liam O'Rourke: Right now it’s configured in the policy engine on our side. We can share the current values and adjust. Longer term we’re adding more visibility in Console.

[08:00] Nikhil Sharma: And for top enterprise routes, we typically set it based on your expected steady-state plus a burst factor, so you don’t get penalized for normal variance.

[08:10] Erin Wallace: Okay. Because we do have a predictable daily peak, but we also have spiky user behavior—like shift change.

[08:18] Rafael Mendes: That’s exactly what burst is for. The risk is when burst combines with fast retries.

[08:25] Erin Wallace: Yeah.

[08:26] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk specifics: since enablement, how has p95 latency been?

[08:31] Erin Wallace: Better. Before, we’d see p95 jump from like 1.2s to 6s during turbulence. Now it’s more like 1.3 to 2.0, and then we see 429 instead of just hanging. That’s arguably better for UX.

[08:46] Priya Desai: Yeah, it’s “fail fast,” not “fail slow.”

[08:50] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly. That’s the intent.

[08:54] Miguel Santos: But our product team sees any 429 as a “provider issue,” so we want to make sure we’re handling it correctly.

[09:02] Liam O'Rourke: Totally fair. Part of this is aligning the semantics. A 429 with Retry-After is basically “we’re up, you should slow down,” not “we’re down.”

[09:14] Erin Wallace: Can we expose the Retry-After to our frontend? We can, but we need to decide.

[09:19] Nikhil Sharma: If it’s the clinician app, I’d recommend not blocking the UI for the full time; better is to show a quick “retrying” and maybe cap at a couple seconds then ask user to retry, depending on workflow.

[09:33] Priya Desai: For our use case, we might want a fallback message after, say, two retries.

[09:39] Erin Wallace: Yeah.

[09:41] Rafael Mendes: Also, if you reduce max_tokens under load, that reduces your GPU decode time, which helps in overload scenarios.

[09:50] Miguel Santos: How should we pick thresholds? Like if we get 429 rate above X then cut max_tokens?

[09:56] Rafael Mendes: That’s a good heuristic. Something like: if 429 rate exceeds 0.5% over 1 minute, reduce max_tokens to, say, 256 for that minute. But we should tune based on your workload. I can share what other customers do generally.

[10:13] Liam O'Rourke: Rafael, can you also explain the enterprise lane behavior during a region dip? Because I think they were expecting “we’re always protected.”

[10:21] Rafael Mendes: Yeah. So the enterprise lane reserves capacity relative to self-serve. But it doesn’t create capacity out of thin air. If a region loses a chunk of GPUs or a kernel regression reduces throughput, then the enterprise lane will still shed. The key is it should shed later and more gracefully than everyone else.

[10:40] Erin Wallace: Makes sense.

[10:42] Miguel Santos: And does it affect other customers first?

[10:45] Rafael Mendes: In broad terms, yes—lower tier traffic is throttled earlier, so enterprise maintains SLO longer.

[10:53] Priya Desai: Okay. So our main lever is to behave nicely: less aggressive retries, respect Retry-After, reduce concurrency.

[11:01] Nikhil Sharma: Yes. And we’ll tune the per-route limit to match your peak plus burst.

[11:07] Erin Wallace: On our side, we can also cap “in flight” requests per user session. Right now it’s basically uncapped.

[11:14] Miguel Santos: It’s like each client can open multiple streams. That might be part of it.

[11:19] Rafael Mendes: That’s a big one. The system tends to fall over when you have high fan-out with retries.

[11:25] Liam O'Rourke: Erin, do you have a rough idea of peak RPS during that window?

[11:29] Erin Wallace: At the application layer, we saw about 220 RPS hitting Redwood. But with retries I think it was higher, maybe 300-ish.

[11:40] Rafael Mendes: Okay, that’s consistent with what I recall; I’ll verify.

[11:44] Miguel Santos: Another odd thing: we saw 429s but latency was not terrible. So it felt like “why throttle if it’s fast.”

[11:53] Rafael Mendes: Yeah that’s a classic. We throttle based on leading indicators too—queue depth, prefill saturation—so we start shedding before latency explodes.

[12:04] Erin Wallace: Okay, preemptive.

[12:06] Rafael Mendes: Exactly.

[12:08] Nikhil Sharma: It’s basically to avoid tail latency and timeouts. The “fast 429” is intentional.

[12:16] Priya Desai: Is there a way to know if the 429 is “your limit” versus “global overload” without parsing strings?

[12:23] Nikhil Sharma: We’re moving toward standardized reason codes. You might already see a field like reason_code. If not, we can confirm what you’re getting. Also the headers: we sometimes include something like x-throttle-reason. Not sure if your SDK surfaces it.

[12:38] Erin Wallace: We’re just using raw HTTP right now.

[12:40] Miguel Santos: We can inspect headers, yeah.

[12:43] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll send a doc snippet listing the exact headers and fields and what to do.

[12:48] Erin Wallace: That’d be great.

[12:50] (crosstalk)

[12:51] Priya Desai: Also—sorry—how does quota play into this? We don’t think we hit quota.

[12:57] Rafael Mendes: You didn’t. Quota 429 would be sustained and would show “quota_exceeded” basically. Your case was spiky and aligned with a burst.

[13:08] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[13:10] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s switch to “what do we do now.” Rafael can pull the exact breakdown for that window. In parallel, on our side, we can consider a temporary burst increase for that one route while you change retry behavior. Does that help, or do you prefer no config changes until you patch the client?

[13:27] Erin Wallace: A temporary increase would help. Our patch will take like a week to roll through mobile.

[13:34] Priya Desai: Yeah, anything that reduces immediate pain.

[13:37] Rafael Mendes: Okay. We can do a modest bump. But I want to be careful not to just allow an unhealthy retry pattern to hit the fleet. So: we’ll bump burst, not the sustained rate.

[13:50] Erin Wallace: That’s fine.

[13:52] Miguel Santos: Can you explain burst versus sustained? Just so I can relay.

[13:57] Rafael Mendes: Sustained is the average allowed per second. Burst is a small buffer—like you can exceed sustained for a short time without being throttled, as long as you’re not doing it continuously.

[14:10] Miguel Santos: Token bucket basically.

[14:12] Rafael Mendes: Yes, token bucket.

[14:14] Nikhil Sharma: And for your kind of shift-change traffic, burst helps a lot.

[14:19] Erin Wallace: Great.

[14:21] Liam O'Rourke: Any other concerns or weird behaviors? You mentioned eu-west having some 429 but less.

[14:28] Miguel Santos: Yeah. We saw maybe a minute where eu-west started returning 429 but then it stopped. That was confusing because we weren’t routing there much.

[14:38] Rafael Mendes: That could be because your failover health checks briefly shifted traffic, or because config propagation wasn’t instantaneous and you had a different policy value between regions for a short time. We’ve had issues where policy updates take a few minutes to converge.

[14:54] Miguel Santos: That’s… plausible.

[14:56] Erin Wallace: We did see some traffic shift, actually.

[14:59] Liam O'Rourke: If it’s propagation delay, we can also look at that. It’s a known risk area.

[15:04] Priya Desai: Is there any risk in us increasing our failover sensitivity to 429?

[15:09] Rafael Mendes: The risk is you could oscillate and amplify load across regions. If you do it, do it with hysteresis—like, only fail over if “over_capacity” persists for N seconds and recover slowly.

[15:23] Erin Wallace: Got it.

[15:25] Nikhil Sharma: And ideally use the reason code. “rate_limit” shouldn’t trigger region failover. “over_capacity” might.

[15:33] Miguel Santos: So we need to parse reason codes anyway.

[15:36] Nikhil Sharma: For now, yes.

[15:38] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll provide the mapping. And longer term we’re adding more stable fields.

[15:44] Erin Wallace: Okay.

[15:46] Liam O'Rourke: Erin, can I ask—did you evaluate other providers for this workload? Just to understand what “good” looks like for your stakeholders.

[15:54] Erin Wallace: We tested Bedrock briefly. And, like, OpenAI obviously. The thing we like about you is performance and the dedicated story. But the product folks compare error rates across vendors.

[16:07] Priya Desai: Yeah, and they interpret 429 as downtime, which is not accurate, but that’s what we’re dealing with.

[16:14] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. We can help with stakeholder messaging. 429 is backpressure, not an outage. But we’ll also work to keep it low.

[16:24] Rafael Mendes: And for context: the protections we enabled should reduce the chance you see 5xx or timeouts during regional stress. So it’s a tradeoff: fewer catastrophic failures, more explicit backpressure.

[16:38] Erin Wallace: That’s a good way to describe it.

[16:41] Miguel Santos: From SRE side, I like 429 more than timeouts.

[16:44] Priya Desai: Same.

[16:46] Liam O'Rourke: Great.

[16:48] Nikhil Sharma: Can I ask about your current retry logic specifics? Like, is it exponential already?

[16:54] Erin Wallace: No. It’s a fixed 200ms then 200ms then 500ms then 500ms then 1s.

[17:02] Nikhil Sharma: Okay. And any jitter?

[17:04] Erin Wallace: None.

[17:06] Nikhil Sharma: I’d strongly recommend jitter. Also, don’t retry streaming requests from scratch unless you have to; it can double your load. If it’s a mid-stream failure, it’s tricky.

[17:18] Erin Wallace: Yeah. We basically restart the whole request.

[17:21] Miguel Santos: We also do something called hedging for one internal service—sending a second request after 300ms. We don’t do it for Redwood… I think. I need to confirm.

[17:33] Rafael Mendes: Hedged requests on LLM calls can be extremely expensive. So if you have that anywhere in the path, please disable for this route.

[17:41] Miguel Santos: Noted.

[17:43] Priya Desai: We can check.

[17:45] Liam O'Rourke: This is a great example of why we’re doing this program. The system can handle high load, but not if the client behavior turns every small blip into 5x traffic.

[17:56] Erin Wallace: Totally.

[17:58] Liam O'Rourke: Rafael, what’s the timeline on your metrics readout?

[18:01] Rafael Mendes: If I get sample request IDs today, I can send a summary tomorrow. Even without IDs, I can pull route-level metrics, but IDs help confirm reason codes.

[18:12] Miguel Santos: I’ll email them right after.

[18:14] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect.

[18:16] Priya Desai: What about visibility in Console? My engineers keep asking for a dashboard.

[18:21] Liam O'Rourke: Today, it’s mostly internal, but we can share screenshots and we can also set up a weekly report if needed. There’s work underway for customer-facing views.

[18:33] Nikhil Sharma: Yeah, we have a design in progress for showing throttling events and limits per route. Not GA yet.

[18:39] Erin Wallace: Okay. We can live with screenshots for now.

[18:43] Miguel Santos: Can we at least get the current limit numbers? Like what’s the RPS and burst.

[18:47] Rafael Mendes: Yes. I’ll include it in the readout and propose the temporary burst increase.

[18:54] Erin Wallace: Great.

[18:56] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else you want to cover? Maybe the semantics for “Retry-After”—is it seconds? milliseconds?

[19:03] Nikhil Sharma: It’s seconds per HTTP spec. Some clients misinterpret it. Make sure your parser treats it as seconds. Sometimes we send an integer, sometimes a date; currently we send integer seconds.

[19:16] Erin Wallace: Good call. We assumed milliseconds in one place. That might be… yeah.

[19:22] Miguel Santos: Oh wow. That would explain some weirdness.

[19:25] Priya Desai: That’s important.

[19:27] Liam O'Rourke: Great catch. That alone might reduce load.

[19:31] Erin Wallace: Yeah.

[19:33] Rafael Mendes: If you were treating 2 seconds as 2 milliseconds, that’s basically a retry storm generator.

[19:38] Erin Wallace: Yeah, yikes.

[19:40] (crosstalk)

[19:41] Erin Wallace: We’ll fix that.

[19:43] Nikhil Sharma: Please do.

[19:45] Liam O'Rourke: Okay. Let’s do a quick recap.

[19:48] Liam O'Rourke: 1) You saw ~1.5% 429 on Feb 4, mostly us-east on /v1/chat/completions.
2) Likely combination of per-route rate limit plus aggressive retry policy.
3) You’ll update client to honor Retry-After (seconds) and add exponential backoff with jitter, reduce retries, and cap in-flight.
4) Redwood will send reason code mapping + retry guidance, and Rafael will pull metrics and propose a temporary burst increase.

[20:18] Priya Desai: That sounds right.

[20:20] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[20:21] Erin Wallace: Yep.

[20:23] Liam O'Rourke: Before we drop, can we agree on a follow-up time? Maybe next Thursday same time?

[20:30] Priya Desai: Next Thursday works.

[20:32] Erin Wallace: Yep.

[20:34] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[20:36] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We’ll send an invite.

[20:39] Nikhil Sharma: And I’ll send the doc snippet today.

[20:42] Rafael Mendes: And I’ll wait for the request IDs and send readout tomorrow.

[20:46] Erin Wallace: Awesome. Thanks all.

[20:49] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[20:50] Miguel Santos: Thanks.

[20:52] Liam O'Rourke: Thanks everyone.

(Recording ended)
